El Nino

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
El Niño 2015/16 is said to be the most extreme ever experienced in recorded history because it coincides with the highest temperatures ever recorded on earth. El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon occurring anything between two and seven years, which can last up to two years at a time. It’s a massive heat system that builds up in the ocean and is an oscillation between an El Niño and a La Niña. Scientists are divided as to what actually triggers the build-up.
El Niño – literally ‘the Christ child’ as it usually hits around Christmas – is caused when the Pacific Ocean warms up over a prolonged period of time, and this leads to a reduction in the easterly trade winds, which in turn reduces the upwelling of cold nutrient-rich deep water. This has a direct impact on southern African weather systems, reducing the number of high pressure systems moving across the south of the continent, which in turn leads to far fewer rain storms in the summer rainfall areas.
La Niña – literally the ‘girl child’ – often follows, and the results can be equally catastrophic for southern Africa. La Niña is the opposite of El Niño, and is caused by a drop in the Pacific Ocean temperatures of between 3 to 5°C. It causes far heavier than normal rainfall in the southern African summer rainfall season, which is normally not catastrophic, but following on a severe drought when there is little or no ground cover, this can lead to massive soil erosion, unchecked flooding, and loss of life and livestock.
Such a massive reorganisation of atmospheric convection, which we define as an extreme El Niño, has severely disrupted global weather patterns, affecting ecosystems, agriculture, tropical cyclones, drought, bushfires, floods and other extreme weather events worldwide. . El Niño is a global weather system bringing extreme rain to some parts and extreme drought to others. For example Southern Africa is crippled by drought but parts of East Africa are drowning in torrential rains.


Further information:
The impact of the El Niño is what scientists find the most difficult to forecast because a strong El Niño does not always result in a severe drought and a weak El Niño does not always result in a mild drought. But the last 10 droughts in Southern Africa were linked to eight El Niños. The drought we experienced last year is directly impacting the severity of the drought we are experiencing this year.
The effect of El Niño on droughts has been exacerbated over the past 50 years. This has been because continental and oceanic temperatures have risen globally but not uniformly due to the increase in carbon dioxide.
SA is at the end of the current El Niño season so we have six months before summer comes to forecast the strength of the El Niño. There are 70 moorings in the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean measuring sea temperature with hundreds of scientists across the globe observing this data as well as satellite images of the oceans. But like all weather forecasting, it remains extremely complex to predict precise rainfall levels.
Although the El Niño effect has been monitored over the last 20 years, we still can’t predict the next 10 to 20 year cycle, but using advanced mapping systems, we are able predict long term weather giving us a picture of the next few months, and even up to a year’s advance warning. This helps with regional mitigation measures.
The link between the El Niño effect and climate change is that scientists are predicting that they may occur with more frequency and with more intensity. This will reduce the recovery period between El Niños and with climate change impacts, ecosystems may not have sufficient time to recover before El Niño strikes again. Whereas the previous, natural cycle helped build the resilience of the system, making it stronger, now we’re weakening the system by having it occur more frequently than the system has evolved to cope with.

Speaking to UN Food Aid Director Brenda Barton she says the biggest problem is that we haven't begun to experience the effects of El Nino yet the food crisis in Southern Africa especially in places like Malawi is from last years drought.

In the United States, there have been record breaking temperatures in the Midwest and the Northeast, there have been stronger than usual, deadly tornadoes and heavy flooding in the Midwest and Southeast, and southern California has been – and still is being – hammered by violent storms and torrential rains.
Further south, Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil have been hit by the worst flooding in 50 years leaving some 150 000 people homeless, while the opposite has happened in Indonesia. There, more than 100 000 fires have choked the region with dense smoke. The fires are lit every year to clear land for palm oil plantations, but this year, a devastating El Niño-linked drought has meant the fires are far worse than usual.
In the United Kingdom, meteorologists say that several strong winter storms, including “Desmond” and “Frank” which led to widespread, disastrous flooding and killed several people, were linked to El Niño.

We are facing the biggest humanitarian crisis across the globe and its coming on the back of other global crisis like in the Middle east. Europe immigrant crisis, the weakening currency because of the decline in the Chinese economy. Aid agencies are competing for the some pot of money. We are looking at a food crisis well into 2017 AND THEN El Nino will more than likely be followed by La Nina which will bring massive flooding. Poor people who live in flood prone areas like in Mozambique already don't move out of flood zones so when La Nina strikes we will see even more chaos.

Press Release:


El Niño
From cyclones in the Pacific and deadly floods in the USA to soaring temperatures fuelling Central American and Southern African droughts and raging fires in Australia, the planet is reeling in the wake of extreme weather conditions. A new El Niño phenomenon has gripped the world’s weather patterns and triggered a large-scale humanitarian crisis. Carte Blanche investigates this radical climate cycle.


Script:


A monster El Nino is causing havoc across the globe. Floods in Paraguay, torrential rains in California, bush fires across Australia and Indonesia, severe drought in Southern Africa and parts of India. The last mega El Nino in 1997/98 had massive social and environmental impacts costing over 33 billion dollars. Ten years later, this El Nino is happening in a significantly warmer climate.
Chris “This El Nino event is coming on the back of very poor harvest for the 2014, 2015 cropping year. Something like 40% in the case of Zimbabwe, nearly 30% in SA and now followed by an El Nino event which we know historically is going to lead to even a poorer harvest. So we have if you will, a double whammy. We are really worried that this is going to be a very bad situation
Script: Chris Nikoi Regional Director for Southern Africa of the United Nations World Food Programme says he expecting the crisis to continue well into 2017
Chris “2 out of every 5 children is malnourished, just imagine the implications of yet a further crisis as a result of El Nino on children. 40 million people in our region and this does not include South Africa are already not meeting their calorific needs and this number before we reach the end of the year could double
Stephen O’Brien” We are here today to re-sound the alarm.”
Script: In New York last week, Stephen O’Brien from the United Nations said the effects are being felt across the globe. They are saying it could be the strongest El Nino yet .
“El Niño tests our commitment to early action, which was reaffirmed after the devastating Horn of Africa drought of 2011. The warning signs are there. Are we prepared to act on them?”
Script: El Nino events happen anywhere between every two and five years and have been with us since the ice age. They’re a complex interaction between the atmosphere and the Pacific Ocean, explains Mathieu Rouault Oceanographer and Climatologist from the University of Cape Town
Mathieu “ If it was not for El Nino, the climate of the tropics and extra tropics would be a lot more stable, still there would be some droughts, still there would be some wet year, but overall there would not that much change. So what’s happening during El Nino is there is a change of location of wet place and dry place, it doesn’t get more extreme, it’s just a change in location of your weather pattern.
Script: Under normal conditions strong westerly trade winds blow across the Pacific ocean moving a warm tongue of water which piles up against the Austro Asian coast. The hot air rises causes heavy rain over the warm water. On the opposite side of the ocean there is an upwelling of cold water and dry air. With an El Nino the westerly wind weakens, and the warm surface water moves back towards the east changing the winds and rainfall.
Mathieu “So it’s not the oceans that start, or the atmosphere that start, it’s the two that are working together and act as a swing that goes from east to west”
Link: El Nino references the Christ child because they normally occur around Christmas time they were first documented by fisherman in the 1600’s who noticed a difference in water temperature and the impact on their fish stocks, but it is only really in the last 50 years that their true impact has been scientifically measured
Script: 70 moored buoys across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans measure ocean temperatures, transmitting data to scientists around the globe. Using satellite images they track the El Nino Southern Oscillation which impacts weather around the Pacific region the strongest
Link: Ocean temperatures were substantially warmer last year than they were during the last super El Nino in 1997/98 but that doesn’t necessarily mean that this current El Nino will have a bigger impact on global weather systems
Mathieu : Another conundrum is that strong El Nino do not necessarily lead to strong drought Sometimes when you have a strong El Nino like in 1997/98 there is little impact, and sometimes, why, when you have a small El Nino, like last year you have a strong impact
Link: This past summer we have seen some of the highest temperatures of the past 150 years. That’s lead some people to draw a link between global climate change and those escalating temperatures. But the more urgent question is what is the impact of Climate change on El Nino?
Script: Director of the Climate and Systems Analysis Group Professor Bruce Hewitson of the University of Cape Town says there is a possibility that the El Nino effect will increase in frequency and strength
Bruce Hewitson: Probably the single strongest signal of global climate change is the heat content of the ocean, and it is just going up and up and up, there’s no pause, there is just a monotonic rise in heat content and that is of course an energy source that drives a lot of the processes, including El Nino, so when El Nino does come along, it is an El Nino on steroids
Script: A strong El Nino is the equivalent energy of 400 000 twenty megaton hydrogen bombs
Bruce: El Nino is in and of itself not a problem, we have historically periodically adapted to El Nino events. It’s the fact that the El Ninos are occurring on top of the back of a warmer, more energetic world that’s concerning because now, the events as a consequence of El Nino, become more serious
Script. We asked Lisa Goddard head of the International Research Institute for Society and Climate at Columbia University, if El Nino events give us a window into the future
Lisa “The impacts of Climate Change are likely quite different from what we see during El Nino events and also the regional understanding of Climate Change is still very uncertain and so I think that drawing too much parallel between climate change and El Nino may be misleading
Script: Climate science has made dramatic advances in the last 10 years improving short term weather forecasts. With a complex mapping system they can also do longer forecasts over a couple of months or a year which are the most accurate during El Nino events. Six months ago Scientist were already warning us about the El Nino
Link: You might think that because El Nino has a specific life span a beginning and an end that its effects would follow that time line but countries have specific contexts such as the drought prone southern Africa for example that means El Nino’s impacts are often felt for years at a time
Chris: In KZN alone something like 40 000 cattle are reported to have died.It takes about 5 to 7 years to have new heifer that will grow into mature cattle that will produce so the depletion of assets which will make these communities and households even poorer will also be something its impact will last for several years. Not to mention the poor rains have led to low levels of water affecting electricity production in many countries in the region, Zambia Zimbabwe just to name a few.
Script: So the more frequently El Nino events occur the less time people and the environment have to recover and adapt. The Ocean is like a massive swing it can return to a stable state after and El Nino, or not.
Link: La Nina which means the girl in Spanish often follows an El Nino event generally it has the opposite impact so for example an area that had been through a significant drought is often battered by torrential rain
Chris “When I mentioned that the impact of this El Nino will be with us not just through 2016 but well into 2017, I was actually being a little optimistic that this El Nino it is not followed by an La Nina, if it is large scale flooding is as bad for agriculture etc as drought
Script: People often incorrectly ascribe all extreme weather events to El Nino
Mathieu: The Scotland flood it is not El Nino because it is not known or demonstrated that El Nino has an impact in Scotland .What is happening is every catastrophe that is the impact of El Nino. He is the fall guy now.
Script: If Governments and Aid agencies had access to the cutting edge of climate science they would be better prepared, in 2015 the International Research Institute hosted a summit on the impacts of El Nino
Lisa “I think there is a realization that it is not just having good science and good information and you actually you need all the experts in between the science and the decision that is based on that science to be involved they need to understand the information they need to have the right policies in place they need to be talking to each other
Bruce: The scary point is how the additional stress of Climate change pushes us closer to a threshold of other things, because when you cross a threshold that part of the system collapses. Imagine a city that can’t supply fresh water, imagine a city that can’t even do sewerage, We need to anticipate them and put in place the various measures that will build resilience against this.
Chris “We have known since last year that we were in an El Nino year but it is unlike an earthquake or a sudden storm it is a slow moving if you will, emergency that builds up gradually
Script: The UN World Food program only has a third of what it needs to cover the looming shortages and the true impact of El Nino is still to come. The world is crippled by major events like Syria, the Middle East and the refugee crisis in a sluggish global economy.
Chris “These huge crisis with political dimensions are dwarfing the attention that needs to be paid to these slow onset emergencies such as the El Nino. I think we are really competing for the funding that we need and I hope that concerned governments begin to step up to the plate
Bruce “Something that affects Bangladesh, is going to affect migration, and if we think the migration into Europe at the moment is bad, that’s just the tip of the iceberg of what could happen in the future. The next generation has a really tough time ahead of them, it doesn’t mean doom and gloom for the long term, but we face a difficult future at this point

They’re a complex interaction between the atmosphere and the Pacific Ocean, explains Mathieu Rouault Oceanographer and Climatologist from the University of Cape Town Mathieu “ If it was not for El Nino, the climate of the tropics and extra tropics would be a lot more stable, still there would be some droughts, still there would be some wet year, but overall there would not that much change. So what’s happening during El Nino is there is a change of location of wet place and dry place, it doesn’t get more extreme, it’s just a change in location of your weather pattern. Script: Under normal conditions strong westerly trade winds blow across the Pacific ocean moving a warm tongue of water which piles up against the Austro Asian coast. The hot air rises causes heavy rain over the warm water. On the opposite side of the ocean there is an upwelling of cold water and dry air. With an El Nino the westerly wind weakens, and the warm surface water moves back towards the east changing the winds and rainfall. Mathieu “So it’s not the oceans that start, or the atmosphere that start, it’s the two that are working together and act as a swing that goes from east to west” Link: El Nino references the Christ child because they normally occur around Christmas time they were first documented by fisherman in the 1600’s who noticed a difference in water temperature and the impact on their fish stocks, but it is only really in the last 50 years that their true impact has been scientifically measured Script: 70 moored buoys across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans measure ocean temperatures, transmitting data to scientists around the globe. Using satellite images they track the El Nino Southern Oscillation which impacts weather around the Pacific region the strongest Link: Ocean temperatures were substantially warmer last year than they were during the last super El Nino in 1997/98 but that doesn’t necessarily mean that this current El Nino will have a bigger impact on global weather systems Mathieu : Another conundrum is that strong El Nino do not necessarily lead to strong drought Sometimes when you have a strong El Nino like in 1997/98 there is little impact, and sometimes, why, when you have a small El Nino, like last year you have a strong impact Link: This past summer we have seen some of the highest temperatures of the past 150 years. That’s lead some people to draw a link between global climate change and those escalating temperatures. But the more urgent question is what is the impact of Climate change on El Nino? Script: Director of the Climate and Systems Analysis Group Professor Bruce Hewitson of the University of Cape Town says there is a possibility that the El Nino effect will increase in frequency and strength Bruce Hewitson: Probably the single strongest signal of global climate change is the heat content of the ocean, and it is just going up and up and up, there’s no pause, there is just a monotonic rise in heat content and that is of course an energy source that drives a lot of the processes, including El Nino, so when El Nino does come along, it is an El Nino on steroids Script: A strong El Nino is the equivalent energy of 400 000 twenty megaton hydrogen bombs Bruce: El Nino is in and of itself not a problem, we have historically periodically adapted to El Nino events. It’s the fact that the El Ninos are occurring on top of the back of a warmer, more energetic world that’s concerning because now, the events as a consequence of El Nino, become more serious Script. We asked Lisa Goddard head of the International Research Institute for Society and Climate at Columbia University, if El Nino events give us a window into the future Lisa “The impacts of Climate Change are likely quite different from what we see during El Nino events and also the regional understanding of Climate Change is still very uncertain and so I think that drawing too much parallel between climate change and El Nino may be misleading Script: Climate science has made dramatic advances in the last 10 years improving short term weather forecasts. With a complex mapping system they can also do longer forecasts over a couple of months or a year which are the most accurate during El Nino events. Six months ago Scientist were already warning us about the El Nino Link: You might think that because El Nino has a specific life span a beginning and an end that its effects would follow that time line but countries have specific contexts such as the drought prone southern Africa for example that means El Nino’s impacts are often felt for years at a time Chris: In KZN alone something like 40 000 cattle are reported to have died.It takes about 5 to 7 years to have new heifer that will grow into mature cattle that will produce so the depletion of assets which will make these communities and households even poorer will also be something its impact will last for several years. Not to mention the poor rains have led to low levels of water affecting electricity production in many countries in the region, Zambia Zimbabwe just to name a few. Script: So the more frequently El Nino events occur the less time people and the environment have to recover and adapt. The Ocean is like a massive swing it can return to a stable state after and El Nino, or not. Link: La Nina which means the girl in Spanish often follows an El Nino event generally it has the opposite impact so for example an area that had been through a significant drought is often battered by torrential rain Chris “When I mentioned that the impact of this El Nino will be with us not just through 2016 but well into 2017, I was actually being a little optimistic that this El Nino it is not followed by an La Nina, if it is large scale flooding is as bad for agriculture etc as drought Script: People often incorrectly ascribe all extreme weather events to El Nino Mathieu: The Scotland flood it is not El Nino because it is not known or demonstrated that El Nino has an impact in Scotland .What is happening is every catastrophe that is the impact of El Nino. He is the fall guy now. Script: If Governments and Aid agencies had access to the cutting edge of climate science they would be better prepared, in 2015 the International Research Institute hosted a summit on the impacts of El Nino Lisa “I think there is a realization that it is not just having good science and good information and you actually you need all the experts in between the science and the decision that is based on that science to be involved they need to understand the information they need to have the right policies in place they need to be talking to each other Bruce: The scary point is how the additional stress of Climate change pushes us closer to a threshold of other things, because when you cross a threshold that part of the system collapses. Imagine a city that can’t supply fresh water, imagine a city that can’t even do sewerage, We need to anticipate them and put in place the various measures that will build resilience against this. Chris “We have known since last year that we were in an El Nino year but it is unlike an earthquake or a sudden storm it is a slow moving if you will, emergency that builds up gradually Script: The UN World Food program only has a third of what it needs to cover the looming shortages and the true impact of El Nino is still to come. The world is crippled by major events like Syria, the Middle East and the refugee crisis in a sluggish global economy. Chris “These huge crisis with political dimensions are dwarfing the attention that needs to be paid to these slow onset emergencies such as the El Nino. I think we are really competing for the funding that we need and I hope that concerned governments begin to step up to the plate Bruce “Something that affects Bangladesh, is going to affect migration, and if we think the migration into Europe at the moment is bad, that’s just the tip of the iceberg of what could happen in the future. The next generation has a really tough time ahead of them, it doesn’t mean doom and gloom for the long term, but we face a difficult future at this point Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for El Nino (4689 ) lizfish@iafrica.com 16 January 2016

metadata.Summary: El Niño 2015/16 is said to be the most extreme ever experienced in recorded history because it coincides with the highest temperatures ever recorded on earth. El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon occurring anything between two and seven years, which can last up to two years at a time. It’s a massive heat system that builds up in the ocean and is an oscillation between an El Niño and a La Niña. Scientists are divided as to what actually triggers the build-up. El Niño – literally ‘the Christ child’ as it usually hits around Christmas – is caused when the Pacific Ocean warms up over a prolonged period of time, and this leads to a reduction in the easterly trade winds, which in turn reduces the upwelling of cold nutrient-rich deep water. This has a direct impact on southern African weather systems, reducing the number of high pressure systems moving across the south of the continent, which in turn leads to far fewer rain storms in the summer rainfall areas. La Niña – literally the ‘girl child’ – often follows, and the results can be equally catastrophic for southern Africa. La Niña is the opposite of El Niño, and is caused by a drop in the Pacific Ocean temperatures of between 3 to 5°C. It causes far heavier than normal rainfall in the southern African summer rainfall season, which is normally not catastrophic, but following on a severe drought when there is little or no ground cover, this can lead to massive soil erosion, unchecked flooding, and loss of life and livestock. Such a massive reorganisation of atmospheric convection, which we define as an extreme El Niño, has severely disrupted global weather patterns, affecting ecosystems, agriculture, tropical cyclones, drought, bushfires, floods and other extreme weather events worldwide. . El Niño is a global weather system bringing extreme rain to some parts and extreme drought to others. For example Southern Africa is crippled by drought but parts of East Africa are drowning in torrential rains.
metadata.Further information: The impact of the El Niño is what scientists find the most difficult to forecast because a strong El Niño does not always result in a severe drought and a weak El Niño does not always result in a mild drought. But the last 10 droughts in Southern Africa were linked to eight El Niños. The drought we experienced last year is directly impacting the severity of the drought we are experiencing this year. The effect of El Niño on droughts has been exacerbated over the past 50 years. This has been because continental and oceanic temperatures have risen globally but not uniformly due to the increase in carbon dioxide. SA is at the end of the current El Niño season so we have six months before summer comes to forecast the strength of the El Niño. There are 70 moorings in the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean measuring sea temperature with hundreds of scientists across the globe observing this data as well as satellite images of the oceans. But like all weather forecasting, it remains extremely complex to predict precise rainfall levels. Although the El Niño effect has been monitored over the last 20 years, we still can’t predict the next 10 to 20 year cycle, but using advanced mapping systems, we are able predict long term weather giving us a picture of the next few months, and even up to a year’s advance warning. This helps with regional mitigation measures. The link between the El Niño effect and climate change is that scientists are predicting that they may occur with more frequency and with more intensity. This will reduce the recovery period between El Niños and with climate change impacts, ecosystems may not have sufficient time to recover before El Niño strikes again. Whereas the previous, natural cycle helped build the resilience of the system, making it stronger, now we’re weakening the system by having it occur more frequently than the system has evolved to cope with. Speaking to UN Food Aid Director Brenda Barton she says the biggest problem is that we haven't begun to experience the effects of El Nino yet the food crisis in Southern Africa especially in places like Malawi is from last years drought. In the United States, there have been record breaking temperatures in the Midwest and the Northeast, there have been stronger than usual, deadly tornadoes and heavy flooding in the Midwest and Southeast, and southern California has been – and still is being – hammered by violent storms and torrential rains. Further south, Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil have been hit by the worst flooding in 50 years leaving some 150 000 people homeless, while the opposite has happened in Indonesia. There, more than 100 000 fires have choked the region with dense smoke. The fires are lit every year to clear land for palm oil plantations, but this year, a devastating El Niño-linked drought has meant the fires are far worse than usual. In the United Kingdom, meteorologists say that several strong winter storms, including “Desmond” and “Frank” which led to widespread, disastrous flooding and killed several people, were linked to El Niño. We are facing the biggest humanitarian crisis across the globe and its coming on the back of other global crisis like in the Middle east. Europe immigrant crisis, the weakening currency because of the decline in the Chinese economy. Aid agencies are competing for the some pot of money. We are looking at a food crisis well into 2017 AND THEN El Nino will more than likely be followed by La Nina which will bring massive flooding. Poor people who live in flood prone areas like in Mozambique already don't move out of flood zones so when La Nina strikes we will see even more chaos.
